lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
For a bounce-height vs ball-type test, name IV, DV, two controls and one possible confounder with a fix.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: Roles correct; confounder realistic with control method.

WATCH FOR
Calling every measured thing independent. IV is what you change on purpose.

teach_steps.example:
WORKED MODEL
If testing insulator type on cooling rate but water volumes differ, volume confounds the result. Fix: same volume and start temperature.

TRY FIRST
For a bounce-height vs ball-type test, name IV, DV, two controls and one possible confounder with a fix.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: Roles correct; confounder realistic with control method.
teach_steps.explain:
Variables: independent (deliberately changed), dependent (measured), controlled (kept constant). Confounding variables accidentally change and weaken conclusions—identify and control them.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on observation, fair tests and design evidence, rather than guessing from a picture alone. Keep every claim linked to what was seen or measured.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the observations, properties or test steps that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a result is uncertain, identify what would have to be observed or tested again. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
teach_steps.notice: Calling every measured thing independent. IV is what you change on purpose. Correct the claim or method, not just the neatness of the diagram.
